passage:
Supervisor's note, written by Pradeep.
Eshaan, twenty-two, our junior analyst, told me over tea that a cousin had asked to borrow money. Eshaan felt obliged, awkward, and afraid the money would not come back, and did not know how to answer. I did not tell Eshaan what to do. I asked what he could give without hardship. He decided on a smaller fixed amount, told the cousin the date he would give it, and said plainly that he could not do more. He put it in a message so both of them remembered. He told me the cousin was quiet, then thanked him. Eshaan looked less tense the next morning.

qa.q: How old is Eshaan?
qa.a: Eshaan is twenty-two.

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling when he told Pradeep about the cousin's request?
qa.a: He felt obliged and awkward, and afraid the money would not come back.

qa.q: What choice did Eshaan make that helped protect both the money and the relationship?
qa.a: He decided on a smaller fixed amount, gave the cousin the date, said plainly he could not do more and wrote it in a message.

qa.q: How might the cousin have felt when Eshaan named the amount and the date?
qa.a: The cousin was quiet and then thanked him, so the cousin probably felt disappointed but also respected by the clear answer.

grounding: A young earner asked for a loan by a cousin feels obligation and fear, and a clear amount and time protects both money and relationship.

passage:
Tuesday night. Farhan Mamu called after dinner. His shop needs money for stock and he asked if I could lend some. My first feeling was pride that he asked me, and then my stomach dropped. I have only just started earning. What if it doesn't come back? What if I say no and Mamu tells the whole family I'm stingy?
I said I would think and call back. Now I have written it down. I can lend one amount that I could manage if it were late, not more. I want a date in writing. I will say I can't promise a second time. Mamu is family, and I still need to be honest.
I will call tomorrow after work.
Zeenat

qa.q: Who called Zeenat after dinner on Tuesday?
qa.a: Farhan Mamu called after dinner.

qa.q: What is Zeenat feeling when thinking about the loan?
qa.a: Zeenat feels torn, proud to be asked, then afraid the money will not come back and anxious about being called stingy.

qa.q: What plan does Zeenat make for answering Mamu?
qa.a: Zeenat plans to offer one amount that would be manageable if it were late, ask for a date in writing, and say plainly that a second loan is not promised.

qa.q: How might Mamu see Zeenat's answer when it comes?
qa.a: Mamu may be disappointed to get only one fixed amount, but he is family and would at least know where he stands with Zeenat.

passage:
Dear Francis,
I need your advice, since you're the most sensible person I know.
My uncle called yesterday. He wants to borrow money from me for his daughter's college admission. I've only been working for eight months. I have a little saved, and I want to help, but I'm scared. Last year he borrowed from my father and still hasn't paid back.
I felt awful saying "let me think." He said, "You've become very big now," and hung up. I've been sick with guilt since.
Here's what I'm thinking: I'll tell him I can give a smaller amount than he asked. I'll say clearly when I'd like it back, and not promise anything more. And I'll talk to my father first, so there are no secrets.
Does that sound fair? I want to protect the relationship, not just the money.
Jahnavi

qa.q: How long has Jahnavi been working?
qa.a: Jahnavi has only been working for eight months.

qa.q: What is Jahnavi feeling after the uncle's call?
qa.a: Jahnavi feels guilty and scared, worried about not being repaid and hurt by the uncle's remark.

qa.q: What choices does Jahnavi consider, and why might they protect the relationship?
qa.a: Jahnavi thinks of offering a smaller amount, stating clearly when it should come back, making no false promises and telling Jahnavi's father first, so expectations stay clear.

qa.q: How might the uncle feel when Jahnavi says "let me think"?
qa.a: The uncle probably felt embarrassed and hurt in his pride, which is why he made a sharp remark and hung up.

grounding: A young earner asked for a loan by an uncle feels obligation and fear of not being repaid, and plans clear terms and no false promises.

passage:
Swati, you asked why my cousin and I still talk, after the loan. Okay, here's the story.
I was twenty-two, just started earning. My cousin Rahat called one night, crying. His bike had broken and he needed money for repairs to keep his delivery job. I felt the obligation in my chest. We'd grown up together.
But I'd seen what loans did in our family. Two uncles haven't spoken in ten years over one.
So I said, "I can give you this much. Please return it by the end of March, in two parts. If you can't, tell me early, and we'll talk." I wrote it in a message so we both had it.
He paid the first part on time. The second was late. He called before the date and said so. I said, "Thanks for telling me." He paid in April.
That's it, Swati. Shalini didn't lose a cousin or the money.

qa.q: Why did Rahat need the money?
qa.a: His bike had broken and he needed money for repairs to keep his delivery job.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling when Rahat called crying?
qa.a: Shalini felt the obligation in her chest, torn between loyalty to a cousin and fear from seeing loans break the family.

qa.q: What made Shalini's approach protect both the money and the relationship?
qa.a: Shalini set a clear amount and time, put it in a message, and invited him to speak early if there was trouble, so there were no false promises.

qa.q: How might Rahat have felt when Shalini thanked him for telling her early?
qa.a: Rahat probably felt relieved and respected, since he was honest about the delay and wasn't blamed.

grounding: A young earner asked for a loan by a cousin feels obligation and fear, and a clear amount and time protect both the money and the relationship.

passage:
Monday. Tushar, twenty-one, three months into his first job, got a call from his cousin Deepak. "Bhai, I need money for my shop's stock. Just till Diwali." Tushar felt his stomach knot. He'd been saving for a course. He said, "Let me think overnight."
Tuesday. He called back. "Deepak, I can give you part of what you asked, not all. I need it back by Diwali. If that's hard, tell me before, not after." Deepak was quiet. "You don't trust me?" Tushar kept his voice warm. "I do. That's why I want it clear, so we never fight." Deepak agreed. Tushar sent a message with the amount and the date.
Diwali. Deepak came with sweets and the money in an envelope. "Stock sold out," he grinned. Tushar hugged him, relieved, and put the envelope straight into his course savings.

qa.q: What did Deepak need the money for?
qa.a: He needed money for his shop's stock.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling when his stomach knotted?
qa.a: Tushar felt anxious and torn, wanting to help Deepak but worried about his own course savings.

qa.q: Why was Tushar's approach a good one?
qa.a: Tushar took time to think, offered a clear amount and time, kept his tone warm and wrote it down, protecting both the money and the relationship.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel when Tushar set terms?
qa.a: Deepak first felt a little hurt, asking if Tushar didn't trust him, but agreed once Tushar explained it was to avoid fights.

grounding: Across several weeks, a young earner asked for a loan by a cousin sets a clear amount and time, protecting both money and relationship.

passage: Sahil, you look like someone whose cousin just asked for money. Sit, I'll tell you mine. I was twenty-two, with my first salary from the bank in Kolkata, when my cousin Tapan came to the house. His shop needed stock before Durga Puja. "Just some, Didi, I'll return it soon." Soon. I felt so awkward I nearly handed him my whole passbook. Instead I asked, "How much exactly, and by when?" He looked hurt. We sat with a paper and wrote down one amount and a date after the Puja sales. I told him plainly, "If it's going to be late, tell me before, not after." He paid half on time and half three months late, but he told me first. We still eat together every Bijoya. Your Bidisha Pishi learnt that soon is not a date.

qa.q: Why did Tapan need money?
qa.a: His shop needed stock before Durga Puja.

qa.q: How did young Bidisha feel when Tapan asked for money?
qa.a: She felt so awkward and obliged that she nearly handed over her whole passbook.

qa.q: At the turning point, what did Bidisha choose instead of handing over the passbook?
qa.a: She asked exactly how much and by when, wrote both down with Tapan, and asked him to warn her before any delay.

qa.q: How might Tapan have felt when Bidisha asked "How much exactly, and by when?"
qa.a: Tapan looked hurt at first, perhaps feeling doubted, but the clear terms later let him stay honest and keep the relationship.

grounding: It illustrates a young earner asked for a loan by a cousin who feels obligation and awkwardness, and protects both money and relationship with clear terms and no vague promises.
